## Potential for further reduction in the embodied carbon in PV solar energy systems

ISSN 1752-1416 Received on 14th August 2015 Revised on 19th October 2015 Accepted on 5th November 2015 doi: 10.1049/iet-rpg.2015.0374 www.ietdl.org

## Stuart J.C. Irvine[1][✉] , Rachael L. Rowlands-Jones[1]

Centre for Solar Energy Research, OpTIC Centre, Glyndwr University, St Asaph, LL17 0JD, UK ✉ E-mail: s.irvine@glyndwr.ac.uk

Abstract: In this study the potential for further reduction in greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) of c-Si, multi-crystalline silicon (mc-Si) and CdTe photovoltaic (PV) systems are assessed to inform climate change mitigation in the UK. The amount of CO2 equivalent released in grams for each kWh of electricity over the lifetime of the PV system (gCO2-e/ kWh) has been assessed using a model to predict the change in GHG as a result of engineering improvements in the PV module and system operation. The scenarios modelled here are for two different locations in the UK (Midlands and South West England) to give a typical range. Similarly a range of carbon intensity in manufacture is considered by taking manufacture in China and the UK. This study considers the impact of; system and inverter lifetimes, continuing trends of increases in module conversion efficiencies and reduction in carbon intensity during manufacture. For most of the scenarios considered the extension of the PV system lifetime to 40 years makes the largest impact while extending inverter lifetime for deployment of thin film PV modules becomes more significant and cannot be ignored. All of the four interventions considered in this study can significantly contribute to a reduction in the carbon footprint of PV by the near term target of 2020. For all three module systems considered the model shows the potential for the carbon footprint to be reduced to one third of the 2012 values giving a range of 11–38 gCO2-e/kWh, which is within the range of current wind generation in the UK.

## 1 Introduction

A considerable body of literature exists on life cycle analysis (LCA) of photovoltaic (PV) solar modules and balance of system components. The carbon footprint of PV systems is largely attributed to the use of energy during manufacture of the components and in particular the PV module. De Wild-Scholten [1] has estimated that for multi-crystalline silicon (mc-Si) the carbon footprint can be as low as 49 gCO2-e/kWh for operation of a roof mounted system in Southern Europe with annual solar insolation of 1700 kWh/m[2] , but three quarters of the carbon contribution comes from the manufacture of the PV cells and the module. The range of carbon footprint estimates can be large depending on where the cells and modules are manufactured and depends on location and orientation of the installed system.

The DECC Solar Strategy: Part II (April 2014) [2] gives a range from 38 gCO2-e/kWh for mc-Si modules manufactured in the UK and system installed in the South West of England to 149 gCO2-e/ kWh for single crystal silicon modules manufactured with a more carbon intense electricity supply in China and the PV system installed in the Midlands with lower solar insolation. This compares with 3–28 gCO2-e/kWh for off-shore and on-shore wind [3], stimulating further work to understand the lifecycle emissions that apply to solar PV deployment in the UK and potential for further reduction in the carbon footprint [2]. The range of embodied carbon emission depends not just on the emission associated with manufacture but also on the energy generated throughout the life of the system. For both wind and solar this depends on the location and will inevitably lead to a wide variation. Siting PV installations in regions of higher solar insolation than the UK results in a lower range than the DECC figures, where 20–81 gCO2-e/kWh has been given as the range from recent studies of installations in South Western United States, Central Europe and Malaysia [1, 4, 5]. The range is still large due to variations in materials, processes and carbon intensity of the electricity used in manufacture.

The LCA methodology for different PV technologies both based on crystalline silicon and thin film PV has been widely reported

[1, 6, 7] and consider the greenhouse gas (GHG) emission throughout the supply chain from mineral extraction through to module installation and end of life decommissioning. Yue et al. [7] have made a comparative study of GHG emission for PV module production in China, which accounts for 62% of the world production of PV modules, and other manufacturing locations such as the USA and Europe. The carbon footprint for manufacture in China was assessed to be approximately twice that of manufacture in Europe with comparative figures of 72.2 and 37.3 gCO2-e/kWh, respectively, for mono-Si and 69.2 and 31.8 gCO2-e/kWh, respectively, for multi-Si. However, assessing the impact of engineering developments for further reduction in carbon footprint and how the local solar insolation will affect it is not easy to assess without going through the whole LCA analysis for each scenario. This paper presents a simple tool to make reasonable estimates of the impact on the carbon footprint from engineering developments in PV systems that are expected over the next few years and puts this in a UK context where there has been a considerable rise in PV adoption due to the UK FiT and falling prices of PV is developing a robust industry for further growth [8].

The current balance of global solar PV market share is approximately 90% silicon with roughly equal share between crystalline silicon (c-Si) and mc-Si [9], with the remainder comprising of inorganic thin film (CdTe, a-Si and CIGS). The dominance of c-Si and mc-Si is largely due to the volume of manufacture [10] and competitive cost per watt combined with a high power output per square metre. The technologies considered in this study are c-Si, mc-Si and CdTe. CdTe was selected as the dominant thin film technology due to the size of its global manufacture and available carbon footprint data, though consideration of other thin film technologies is discussed.

## 2 Model

Different metrics can be used to represent the carbon footprint of a PV system and include energy payback time, carbon payback time

and amortised CO2 emissions over the life of the system. Only the latter takes into account the life of the PV system whereas the energy payback time only considers the period of time taken to equal the amount of energy used in production. Consistent with normal practice in LCA of PV for carbon footprint the amount of CO2 released in grams for each kWh of electricity that the PV system produces (gCO2-e/kWh) is the chosen metric used throughout this paper [1, 3–7]. The energy yield depends on the geographic location, orientation, shading etc. of the PV modules. For the purposes of calculation of energy yield this paper assumes a South facing roof mounted installation with no shading. The geographical location enables an assessment of a typical range between the Midlands and South West, which covers a large proportion of the installed PV, but carbon footprint will increase when assessing installations at lower solar insolation further North in the UK.

The proposed model provides a framework for calculating the improved carbon footprint of PV installations, based on existing LCA data, and allows comparison of:

- (i) Resource inputs and technology.

- (ii) Manufacturing.

- (iii) Location of installation.

- (iv) Sizing and efficiency.

- (v) Operational life.

The PV module technologies considered were, mc-Si, c-Si and CdTe, with starting module conversion efficiencies of 14.1%, 14.8% and 11.9%, respectively (2012 figures [1]). The mc-Si and c-Si starting module efficiencies are average from the 2012 data and appear low by current expectations due to the mix of older manufacturing processes. The model relies on a consistent set of starting data which in this case is taken from that of de Wild-Scholten where the 2013 publication relates to 2012 data. Other start dates can be readily used and updated in the model as new data becomes available but for this paper the 2012 start date provides the most comprehensive data. The initial system and inverter operation lifetimes were considered as 25 years and 10 years, respectively, in line with existing industry warranties, although it is recognised that de Wild-Scholten [1] uses a figure of 30 years this does not affect the GHG emission per kWp of module production/installation which is the input used for this model. Linear degradation factors for the three PV technologies considered were; 0.0023 (c-Si), 0.0059 (mc-Si) and 0.0030 (CdTe), taken from Jordan et al. [11].

The parameters used to assess the current carbon footprint of these solar PV technologies are shown in Table 1. These values are taken from de Wild-Scholten except for the Chinese manufactured CMod values which have been corrected for 2012 Chinese average electricity carbon intensity figure of 760 gCO2-e/kWh rather than the de Wild-Scholten figure of over 1000 gCO2-e/kWh which is applicable to manufacture using electricity just from hard coal. Both the Chinese carbon intensity for electricity production and those used for the UK are taken from the IEA ‘CO2 emissions from fuel combustion Highlights’ 2013 [12]. It can be seen from Table 1 that although the carbon contribution for the module decreases from c-Si through to CdTe due to a reduction in energy used in manufacture, the carbon content for the mounts actually increases. This occurs due to the lower module efficiency of 11.9% for CdTe compared with 14.8% for c-Si which results in a larger area of CdTe modules being used to generate 1 kWp. As the efficiency of these modules improves it is expected that this carbon contribution will decrease and this is reflected in (2).

## 3 Short term improvements in carbon footprint (2020)

Short term improvements in the carbon footprint, based on the currently available PV module technologies, could be achieved with a combination of the following measures:

(i) Extend system lifetime to 40 years which would give end of life outputs for c-Si, mc-Si and CdTe of 91%, 79%, and 88%, respectively, based on the degradation factors given in Table 1.

(ii) Improve inverter lifetime to 25 years based on more durable micro-inverters or improved/serviceable string inverters.

Fig. 1 Average module efficiency of mono and mc-Si and CdTe products from 2000–2014 [22, 23]

(iii) Module conversion efficiency improvements based on current projections to 22%, 20% and 19% for c-Si, mc-Si and CdTe, respectively.

(iv) Reduction in carbon intensity in manufacture of 2.5% and 1.96% per annum for UK and China, respectively, estimated from historical IEA data and trends from 2005 [12].

These factors are seen as being lower risk options in the shorter term but there are other factors such as materials reduction, improving materials and module yield, reduction in energy used in manufacturing etc. All these are accounted for in the model and can be introduced as an engineering tool to assess carbon impact for future improvements in manufacturing. These additional manufacturing improvements are not included in this scenario simply because of the uncertainty of materials reduction by 2020 but there is a considerable body of evidence that silicon cell thickness will reduce, with the potential for 100 μm or less [13, 14]. The amount of reduction is difficult to predict at this stage as the laboratory demonstrations will have to be translated into large volume manufacture. The reduction in silicon cell thickness will be accounted for in the model using the R factor in 4 but this must also account for waste silicon from wafer sawing in addition to the active material in the cells. Reduction in the active layer thickness

in thin film CdTe modules is also possible but is not likely to make a major impact in the short term carbon reduction but offers potential for layer thickness of 1 μm or less in the longer term [15].

Alternative materials such as CZTS and Perovskites are seen as making an impact on a longer timescale as the PV market up to 2020 is going to be dominated by c-Si and mc-Si with around 10% thin film PV which is dominated by CdTe. Some modelling has also been carried out on CIGS which is a rapidly growing module product but the focus here is on CdTe which currently dominates the thin film PV sector of the market and provides an example of what can be achieved with short term developments in thin film PV. A brief summary is given for each of the four improvements considered in this paper.

## 3.1 System lifetime

A key consideration, particularly for commercial and utility scale systems, in achieving maximum power output is the ongoing operation and maintenance of the PV system. PV systems can be kept in service for decades. Increasing system lifetime from 25 to 40 years for low annual degradation rates is likely to be a major contributor to reduced carbon content of solar PV.

Commercial PV modules offer guarantees with a power output of 80% after 25 years, but a number of manufacturers are starting to offer longer warranties. SolarWorld currently offer 30 year warranty with linear output decline to 87% for both c-Si and mc-Si modules [16]. Centrosolar and Solarwatt similarly offer 30 year to 87% performance warranty on their c-Si glass–glass modules [17, 18]. The IEA PVPS task 12 guidelines recommend taking linear degradation over 30 year lifetime. This study has modelled the impact of the system lifetime for 25, 30 and 40 years. First Solar CdTe device platform has a proven track record, with over 18 years of field data [19, 20] and improvements to CdTe-based devices have increased long-term stability enabling the long-term degradation guidance to be −0.5% per annum for all climates [20]. A higher confidence can be expected on the c-Si and mc-Si as operational lifetime has already been achieved on the early manufactured modules.

Applying linear degradation factors (d) outlined in the model for the three PV technologies under investigation, yields linear output decline figures of 91%, 79% and 89%, respectively for c-Si, mc-Si and CdTe with a 40 year lifetime as shown in Table 2 and compared with 25 and 30 year degradation factors. This shows that for all the module technologies considered the projected energy yield after 40 years would justify running these PV systems for at least this period of time and therefore form a key consideration for the potential for carbon mitigation in solar PV.

## 3.3 Module conversion efficiency

Module conversion efficiency for all technologies considered here has historically improved over recent years and this trend is set to continue over the time period of this study. Photon International annually charts the average efficiency of PV module products since 2000 [19]. This data has been plotted with module efficiency data for CdTe [20]. The trend in module efficiency for mc-Si, c-Si and CdTe are shown in Fig. 1.

The efficiency of commercial Si modules over the period 2000– 2014 has been increasing by approximately 1% point every 3 years [19]. If this trend continues then mc-Si modules will have 20% average efficiency and mono-Si modules will have 22% average efficiency by 2020. There is strong evidence to support this continuing trend as leading PV manufacturers already produce some silicon products with module efficiency up to 20% [24]. This is consistent with trends expected by the IEA and reported by Cherrington et al. [8] of 23% for C-Si and 19% for mc-Si.

The efficiency of CdTe commercial modules has also been increasing since 2000. First Solar’s average production module efficiency reached 12.9% Q4 of 2012 and the lead line production of 13.1% module Q4 2012. First Solar module conversion efficiency in production has now reached 14% with a record research module of 17.0% achieved in April 2014 [20]. As a result of these improvements First Solar have extended their module conversion efficiency roadmap to 2017 with an expectation to achieve module conversion efficiencies of 18.1–18.9% by 2017. If this trend continues CdTe module efficiencies to reach 19% by 2020 can be expected, offering a considerable improvement on the 2012 figure of 11.9% used as the starting figure [1].

## 3.2 Inverters

## 3.4 Reduction in carbon intensity during manufacture

The inverter contribution to carbon footprint is relatively small in the de Wild-Scholten model [4] if one neglects the need for inverter replacement over the life of the system. Extending the life of the system will actually increase the carbon footprint contribution from the need for inverter replacement. It is only relatively recent that inverter warranties of 10 years have become common, but still much less than the expected lifetime of the system. The effect of this can be seen in (2) where a system running for 40 years with inverters being replaced every 10 years would quadruple the carbon footprint contribution from the inverter. It is also clear from (1) that as the module contribution decreases, which currently dominates the system carbon footprint, then the inverter contribution becomes more significant. Therefore, the major short term contribution that can be made by the inverter for carbon reduction is to increase the lifetime, continuing the current trend.

String inverters have dominated the solar industry since its inception but the introduction of micro-inverters has marked a significant technology shift within the sector. Several solar companies have launched their own micro-inverters, with the potential to recover 10–20% of the annual loss due to partial shading with increasing gains from systems with multiple parallel strings [21]. Micro-inverters offer advantages through individual optimisation of PV modules enabling each individual PV module to operate at its maximum potential. Micro-inverters are not exposed to as high power and heat loads as central inverters thus generally resulting in longer operating lifetimes. However, there are concerns that they will run hotter due to mounting on the back of the module which could lead to premature failure. More long term experience will be needed and studies on thermal management to verify the predicted lifetimes. Most central inverters currently have guarantees of just 10 years, but engineering to enable replacement of failed components such as electrolytic capacitors will help to extend lifetime.

The carbon intensity during manufacture of the PV modules was considered for country of manufacture, consistent with the methodology used by de Wild-Scholten [1] and Yu et al. [7]. The IEA statistics for CO2 emissions from fuel combustion were used to calculate the average percentage annual decrease in CO2 emissions per kWh from electricity generation between 2005 and 2011 for UK and China [12], resulting in reductions of 1.47% and 2.5% per annum, respectively. Using a linear extrapolation in reduction from the starting year of 2012 to 2020 this results in carbon intensity of 605 and 403 gCO2-e/kWh for China and the UK, respectively, in 2020 which were the ‘improved’ figures used in this model.

## 4 Modelling results for different module types

## 4.1 c-Si modules

Results are presented showing the amortised carbon footprint for systems based on each of the module types and for the assumption of module manufacture in a Chinese or UK carbon intensity environment. For each of these module types an assessment has also been made of the combined effect of all these short term carbon reduction interventions.

The results of the modelling for c-Si manufactured in China and the UK are summarised in Figs. 2a and b, respectively. Each chart shows the baseline carbon footprint based on the model numbers given in Table 1 with separate bars for the Midlands and South West England locations that effectively shows a range according to location of the PV array. Each of the next four sets of bars show the carbon reduction with just one short term carbon mitigation measure and the final set show the combined effect if all these measures are adopted. The largest single opportunity for carbon mitigation for c-Si is increasing system operating lifetimes up to 40 years which is supported by the very low degradation factor for

Fig. 3 Potential carbon reduction for mc-Si manufactured in a China b UK

c-Si of 0.0023, giving a predicted 91% of initial performance after 40 years (Table 2). All the interventions contribute significantly to a reduction in carbon footprint for c-Si with the significant being carbon intensity reduction and extending inverter lifetime. Reduction in carbon intensity is expected to continue in both the Chinese and UK manufacturing scenarios as the proportion of renewable energy increases and older, less efficient fossil fuelled power stations are replaced. The impact of improved inverter lifetime will increase as the module contribution is reduced hence will have a more significant long term impact. The combined effect of these interventions is a dramatic decrease to approximately one third of the initial carbon footprint to 32–38 gCO2-e/kWh for Chinese manufactured modules and 24–28 gCO2-e/kWh for UK manufactured modules. This is consistent with 2014 figures given by Yue et al. [7] of 72 and 37 gCO2-e/kWh when taking into account that the figures given here are projected to 2020 but a higher solar insolation of 1700 kWh/m[2] /annum were used by Yue et al. It is interesting to note that for Yue et al. [7] and de Wild-Scholten [1] the carbon footprint when using Chinese manufactured modules is twice that of the UK manufactured modules whereas the projected figures given here narrow that gap to just 50% higher for the Chinese manufactured modules.

## 4.2 mc-Si modules

The mc-Si carbon footprint is, as expected, lower than for c-Si but the pattern for carbon reduction is similar with the largest single impact being the extended system lifetime, closely followed by module efficiency. The significance of extended inverter lifetime becomes clearer (Fig. 3) with mc-Si than for c-Si, due to the lower

carbon impact of the module manufacture, with that measure alone reducing the carbon emission to less than 45 gCO2-e/kWh for UK manufacture and Midlands location with less than 40 gCO2-e/kWh for the South West location. The combined effect for UK manufacture starts to get down to the figures more typical of thin film PV modules with 17 gCO2-e/kWh for the South West location. The equivalent Chinese manufacture figure is as low as 21 gCO2-e/kWh. The gap between Chinese and UK manufacture has narrowed more than for c-Si as the BOS becomes a more significant part of the total carbon contribution. It is interesting to note that these projected figures, for a UK location, takes the carbon footprint of PV solar to be within the range for nuclear (3–35 gCO2-e/kWh) and wind (3–41 gCO2-e/kWh), at the top end of hydropower (2–20 gCO2-e/kWh) and the bottom end of biomass (8.5–130 gCO2-e/kWh) [3].

## 4.3 CdTe modules

For modules manufactured in the UK (Fig. 4b) the extension of system lifetime to 40 years still has the largest impact but with inverter lifetime along with efficiency giving similar contributions to potential carbon reduction. This is in-line with the expectations where the inverter carbon footprint becomes more significant as the module carbon content is reduced. There is also a negative effect that this has on just extending system lifetime to 40 years without extending the inverter lifetime, more replacements of the inverter are needed during the life of operation. This is illustrated in Fig. 4a where just extending system lifetime to 40 years is slightly higher than just extending inverter lifetime. The combined figures take account of this by extending system lifetime and

Fig. 4 Potential carbon reduction for CdTe manufactured in a China b UK

inverter lifetime. The combined effect of these interventions for CdTe PV system carbon footprint is in the range of 12–14 gCO2-e/kWh for Chinese manufactured modules and 11–12 gCO2-e/kWh for UK manufactured modules. This is consistent with the c-Si and mc-Si module systems and is approximately one third of the 2012 starting values. Predictions by Kim et al. [5] for the effect of increasing the efficiency of the CdTe PV modules from 11.2 to 17.3% showed similar decreases in GHG 27% down to 11 gCO2-e/kWh but the basis for this estimate was for solar insolation of 1810 kWh/m[2] /annum. With the lower solar insolation in the UK it is necessary for the combination of the four interventions assessed in this paper to yield a similar result in the carbon impact. It is also important to note that there is now relatively little difference between Chinese and UK module manufacturing due to the lower energy used per kWp for CdTe thin film modules and the relatively greater contribution from the BOS. A preliminary analysis of CIGS carbon footprint, using the same methodology shows similar reduction to that for CdTe but with slightly higher starting values of 38–45 gCO2-e/kWh for UK manufacture going down to 15–18 gCO2-e/kWh in 2020 by applying the same four set of interventions.

## 5 Conclusions

A model has been presented to enable a prediction of the reduction in GHG emissions for PV solar energy based on anticipated engineering improvements in the PV modules and system operation. Based on four selected interventions the model shows the potential for a substantial reduction of carbon footprint for all the PV module types currently in use. A combination of system improvements including extended system and inverter lifetime, higher module efficiencies and reduction in carbon intensity at the point of manufacture reduces the range of GHG from 30–109 gCO2-e/kWh to 11–38 gCO2-e/kWh in 2020. This is within the range of the carbon footprint for UK wind energy deployment and has the potential for further reduction in the longer term which will be considered in further developments of this model along with the potential impact of new materials and reduction in the primary energy used in PV module manufacture.
